\chapter{Evening}
\label{ch:la-evening}
\hlchaptermodality{33}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say evening in Latin, and follow the vesper root into Hesperia, víspera, and vespers.}

Sort any European evening word into the vesper family or the sērus family, then produce vesper and the everyday vespere Cicero uses for in the evening.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vesper]{vesper — the evening word its own daughters mostly abandoned}

\label{lesson:LA-C33-vesper}



\begin{quote}
A genuinely ordinary Latin word for \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} — and a root that quietly reaches all the way to the English word \emph{west}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Vesper} (also \textbf{vespera}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{evening}\textquotedblright{} — is a genuine, ordinary Classical Latin word, not a rare or poetic one: \textbf{vespere} (\textquotedblleft{}in the evening\textquotedblright{}) shows up routinely in Cicero's own letters. It traces to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*wekero-}} (\textquotedblleft{}evening, night\textquotedblright{}), itself an enlarged form of a root \emph{\textbf{*we-}}, which some reconstructions gloss as \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{} (the direction the sun sets) — though this specific piece is more contested than the vesper/west link itself. That same conceptual root, through a completely separate \textbf{Germanic} branch, gives English its own word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{west}\textquotedblright{} — evening and west, sharing one deep idea: the direction the sun goes down.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vesper\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}evening,\textquotedblright{} genuinely everyday Classical Latin
  \item the deep root — \emph{wekero-}, shared with English \textquotedblleft{}west,\textquotedblright{} the direction of sunset
  \item the careful hedge — a lower root meaning \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{} is more contested
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word shares vesper's deep PIE root, and what's the connecting idea? (\textbf{West} — both trace to the direction the sun sets.) Is the proposed still-deeper root meaning \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{} equally secure? (\textbf{No — that sub-root is more contested than the vesper/west link.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Hesperia, víspera, vespers]{Hesperia, víspera, vespers — the root after Latin}

\label{lesson:LA-C33-vesper-afterlives}



\begin{quote}
Latin \textbf{vesper} and English \textbf{west} share the sunset idea. Now follow the evening root through Greek, English, Spanish, French, and Italian.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Greek hesperos}
The Greek cognate \textbf{hesperos} gives English \textbf{Hesperus}, the evening star (Venus at dusk), and \textbf{Hesperia}, \textquotedblleft{}land of the west.\textquotedblright{} The name is relative: Greeks used it for Italy, west of Greece; Romans could use it for Spain, west of Italy.

\begin{cousinweb}
English borrowed \textbf{vespers}, the evening prayer service, and \textbf{vespertine}, \textquotedblleft{}of the evening,\textquotedblright{} directly from Latin.

Spanish inherited \emph{vespera} as \textbf{víspera}, but narrowed its meaning to \textquotedblleft{}the eve\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}the day before\textquotedblright{} an event. French \textbf{soir} and Italian \textbf{sera} do not descend from \textbf{vesper} at all. They rebuilt \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{sērus}, \textquotedblleft{}late,\textquotedblright{} through the idea of the \textquotedblleft{}late day.\textquotedblright{}

One ordinary Latin word therefore leaves three different outcomes: a learned English loan, a narrowed Spanish descendant, and replacement by a different root in French and Italian.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Hesperia\textquotedblright{} — land of the west
  \item \textquotedblleft{}víspera\textquotedblright{} — the eve or day before, narrowed from evening
  \item \textquotedblleft{}soir, sera\textquotedblright{} — from sērus, \textquotedblleft{}late,\textquotedblright{} not from vesper
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Hesperus? (\textbf{The evening star.}) What does Spanish \textbf{víspera} mean now? (\textbf{The eve or day before an event.}) Which Latin root supplies French \textbf{soir} and Italian \textbf{sera}? (\textbf{Sērus, \textquotedblleft{}late.\textquotedblright{}}) Name one direct English borrowing from \textbf{vesper}. (\textbf{Vespers} or \textbf{vespertine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — sort the evening words, then read the Latin}

\label{lesson:LA-C33-practice}



\begin{quote}
Be honest about what this chapter can give you. There is no Roman \textquotedblleft{}good evening\textquotedblright{} yet — that arrives next chapter, and even then it is modern. What you can do \textbf{today} is triage: hear any European evening word and place it in the right family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the two families, and the test that separates them}
Everything in this chapter falls into exactly two lines, and one question separates them: \textbf{does the word still carry a \emph{v} or an \emph{h} from the sunset root, or does it come from \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}?}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Sunset family} — from \emph{vesper}, or its Greek cousin \emph{hesperos}: vespers, vespertine, víspera, Hesperus, Hesperia.
  \item \textbf{Late family} — from \emph{sērus}, \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}: French \emph{soir}, Italian \emph{sera}.
\end{itemize}

Two traps worth naming. \textbf{Víspera} is in the sunset family but no longer means \textquotedblleft{}evening\textquotedblright{} — it narrowed to \textquotedblleft{}the eve, the day before.\textquotedblright{} And \emph{soir} and \emph{sera} look like the closest heirs of all, being the everyday words in Latin's two nearest daughters, yet they are the ones that are \textbf{not} descended from \emph{vesper} at all.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Sort:} vespers, sera, Hesperus, soir, víspera $\to$ sunset or late
  \item \emph{Say it:} the noun — \textbf{vesper}; and \textquotedblleft{}in the evening\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{vespere}, the form Cicero uses in his letters
  \item \emph{Say it:} the deep link that started it — \emph{vesper} and English \textbf{west}, one idea: where the sun goes down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sort these three without looking: \textbf{vespertine}, \textbf{sera}, \textbf{Hesperia}. (Sunset, late, sunset.) What does \emph{víspera} mean in Spanish now? (\textbf{The eve, the day before} — narrowed, not lost.) And which everyday Latin form means \textquotedblleft{}in the evening\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Vespere}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
